extra_brief:
### Language: Russian is ALWAYS in scope (Baird directive, 2026-08-26)

Uzbekistan's pipeline record is overwhelmingly Russian-language and Soviet-era. **Search in
Russian FIRST and treat it as primary, not as a fallback after English comes up dry.** Uzbek
(Latin script) counts too. English-only searching is how a real source gets missed here.

Where the material actually lives: `uzbekneftegaz.uz`, `utg.uz` (Uzbektransgaz),
`minenergy.uz`, `gov.uz`, `lex.uz` and `norma.uz` (legal acts, decrees, investment programmes
— these name pipelines and lengths), `stat.uz`, plus reporting from `uzdaily.uz`, `gazeta.uz`,
`kun.uz`, `podrobno.uz`, `review.uz`, `trend.az`, `interfax.ru`, `neftegaz.ru`,
`oilcapital.ru`. For the transit trunks, Gazprom and CNPC corporate material. Soviet-era
technical literature (`Газовая промышленность`, VNIIgaz/VNIPItransgaz tables) is legitimate
and often the only place a string's diameter and length are itemised — Ukraine's whole unlock
was one VNIPItransgaz table. Cite the Russian-language page directly; put the English gloss in
researcher_notes and set `source_language` to `ru` or `uz`.

### Calibrate UNRESOLVED honestly — this country sits between India and Kazakhstan

Do not reach for `UNRESOLVED` before you have searched in Russian. But equally, do not
manufacture a citation: these are domestic strings operated by a state monopoly that does not
publish line-wise specs, so after a genuine Russian-language search an honest `UNRESOLVED` on
a per-string diameter or capacity is often the CORRECT outcome (Kazakhstan's reading), not a
failure. What is NOT acceptable is an `UNRESOLVED` that only reflects an English-only search.

### The wiki-citation trap — a harvested URL earns ONE cell, not a row

`wiki_citations.json` is keyed by row, but 18 rows map to only 11 gem.wiki pages, so several
of your candidate URLs were harvested from a page that is about a **parent trunk or a sibling
string**, not about your segment. A URL earns a `[ref]` cell only when the page names **your
segment's own value**. Sharpest case, and it is probably yours: **P6933 / P6934 / P6935**
(`Mubarek-Zirabulak I / II / III`) hang off the Bukhara–Tashkent–Bishkek–Almaty page, whose
own parent rows are **excluded from this batch** — so that page's citations are about the
parent trunk and do NOT support a Mubarek–Zirabulak string's length or diameter. Same shape
for the `Gazli-Kagan`, `Yangiyer-Ahangaran` and `Mubarek-Kagan` string families.

### Two specific hypotheses to TEST (do not assume either is true)

1. **P6933 / P6934 / P6935 carry diameters of exactly 1020, 1021 and 1022 mm.** Three parallel
   strings differing by 1 mm is not a plausible engineering fact; it has the signature of a
   segment index added into the diameter cell. Source each string's real diameter. If Soviet
   practice gives all three as DN1020, that is a `spec` concern on two rows — but SOURCE it,
   do not infer it from the pattern alone.
2. **P2698 Shurtan–Sherabad carries Capacity = 1.00** where every sibling reads 10–35. Check
   whether the true figure is ~1 bcm/y (possible for a regional feeder) or a units/typo defect.

### Duplicates: a parallel string is REAL pipe, not a double count

Every string family here (Gazli-Kagan I–IV, Mubarek-Zirabulak I–III, Yangiyer-Ahangaran I–II,
Mubarek-Kagan I–II) is by construction several pipes in one corridor. **Kazakhstan's cluster A
is the governing lesson:** a duplicate flag there had the aggregate-vs-segment signature AND
lengths agreeing to 0.20 km, and it was still REFUTED, because two official sources named each
string as its own trunk with its own diameter. Only SOURCING decides duplication — matching
lengths, a shared corridor, and a parent/child name pattern are all consistent with genuinely
separate pipe. Flag `duplicate` only when a source affirmatively describes the two rows as one
pipe, and say which source.

### 13 rows are deliberately NOT in this batch

The CAC (Lines A/B/C), Bukhara–Ural, BTBA parents and CA–China trunk rows are excluded because
they are Kazakhstan's rows, already staged there. If a source you find is about one of those
trunks, use it only insofar as it names YOUR row's segment. Never stage anything against
P0739, P0740, P1124, P2289, P2291, P2292, P2299, P2300, P3956, P5695, P5770, P5771, P5810.
(**P2030 CAC Line D is legitimately IN scope** — Line D routes Turkmenistan–Uzbekistan–
Tajikistan–Kyrgyzstan–China, bypassing Kazakhstan, so no other batch carries it.)

### Access failures are NOT deletions — this is a hard rule

Half of this country's existing refs are already dead (39 of 78 filled cells). Even so: **only
a confirmed HTTP 404 or 410 may cause a ref to drop.** A 403, a WAF block, a geo-block, a TLS
failure or a timeout means the page is INACCESSIBLE TO US, which is not evidence it is gone —
keep the ref, say so in researcher_notes, and add a Wayback snapshot ALONGSIDE it rather than
in place of it. Kazakhstan's `adilet.zan.kz` case: an incomplete TLS chain made 51 of 105 ref
cells look dead with zero real 404s.

Known here: `utg.uz/ru/about/history/` is a **confirmed genuine 404**. Its Wayback capture
`20260314231446` exists (the availability API confirms a 200) but `web.archive.org` content
serving was unreachable all of 2026-08-26 from this machine. If it is still unreachable for
you, that is a **network condition and tells you nothing about the source** — do not record it
as missing, and do not cite a capture you could not actually read.

### Anchor-and-endpoint reality

Most of these rows have a blank end location (`->?` in the roster). Endpoints are worth real
effort: they are what make a length checkable. Watch for geocoder-style false matches, the
dominant defect in Ukraine and Egypt — Central Asian toponyms repeat across republics, so
confirm an anchor is in Uzbekistan (or the right oblast) before you trust a distance built on
it. Note that `Operator` for these rows lives on the separate operators/owners tab, not on the
gas tab; your worklist already carries those units where they exist.
